newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia sees short-term ASEAN pain, later gain.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia sees short-term ASEAN pain, later gain.

text.p: Cambodia will reap long-term economic rewards by joining Southeast Asia's regional association but there will be some painful restructuring before any financial benefits begin to flow, officials and analysts said on Friday.

Foreign ministers from the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are meeting in Kuala Lumpur on Saturday to decide when to admit its final three members -- Cambodia, Burma and Laos.

Officials in the region say the three will join Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam as full ASEAN members by the end of the year despite concern about political stability in Cambodia and human rights in Burma.

But before Cambodia sees any benefits from membership of ASEAN and the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA), the state will have to be weaned off an over-reliance on customs revenues and the sluggish export sector will have to be revamped, economic analysts said.

"In the short term there may be some pain," Paul Matthews, resident representative of the U.N. Development Programme told a forum on ASEAN on Friday. "The first years of membership may create problems, there will be some difficult adjustments. In the long term, the people will benefit."

AFTA membership requires the slashing of tariffs on most goods to a maximum of five percent within 10 years but the government currently gets 70 percent of its tax revenue from tariffs compared with less than 20 percent in Thailand and Malaysia and some seven percent in Indonesia, according to finance ministry data.
"In the short run, we suffer a little," Foreign Minister Ung Hout told Reuters. "We have to change our tax system."
Cambodia passed a new tax law earlier this year and the introduction of income tax and a value added tax are both imminent.

"We reduce customs duties gradually, but mind you we don't have to do it next year when we join ASEAN, or this year when we join ASEAN. We will have a programme to do it over a period of 10 years, so it's not a problem," Ung Hout said.
ASEAN membership was inevitable for a small Cambodia sandwiched between large neighbours, Thailand and Vietnam, Ung Huot said.

"We have to do it to survive in the region," he said. "When our neighbours reduce their tariffs, goods will flow to their countries. But if the tariff is too high in Cambodia, the goods will come through smuggling."

Cambodia will have to aim for export-led growth on the back of foreign direct investment (FDI) if it is to benefit from its membership in the dynamic Southeast Asian free trade area, officials and economists say.
"The key to resolving balance of payment and trade issues will be through the promotion of FDI to establish and strengthen the production base," the finance ministry said in a recent paper.
Cambodia was looking to rice and rubber, at least in the short term, to boost export figures, analysts said.
"It's the commodities, agricultural and natural resource based, that is where Cambodia's comparative advantage lies right now," said one economic analyst involved in the ASEAN issue.

"The next step would be some agro-processing and later some light manufacturing -- basic assembly of electronics, televisions, some computer stuff. That kind of light assembly could be a potential winner here," he said.
"Anything that makes it cheaper to bring goods in will make it cheaper to manufacture here," he said.
